required [strong parallel trends]{.alert-blue} --- a substantially stronger
assumption than most researchers realize they are invoking

* We discussed some (sub-)cases where it might be plausible and/or weakened, but it seemed fundamentally difficult to assess as only untreated potential outcomes are observed in pre-treatment periods

[This session:]{.alert} can we use pre-treatment data to say anything about whether (local) strong parallel trends is plausible in a given application?

* Main idea: check for [close comparison groups]{.alert-green} --- neighboring dose groups that have the same level of outcomes in pre-treatment periods, argue that strong parallel trends is more plausible for these groups

# 1. Setup and Discussion of Strong Parallel Trends {visibility="uncounted"}

## Setup

Same [pre-post research design with a continuous treatment]{.alert} as Session 1:

* Two periods $t=1,2$;
* No one treated at $t=1$;
* Continuous dose $D_i$ realized at $t=2$

In order to make the argument that the levels of pre-treatment outcomes are informative about strong parallel trends, we need to think some more about where parallel trends and strong parallel trends come from. →

## Motivating Parallel Trends

The most common way to "more primitively" motivate the parallel trends assumption is as a combination of the following two assumptions [@ashenfelter-card-1985;@angrist-krueger-1999;@ghanem-santanna-wuthrich-2024; @marx-tamer-tang-2025]:

::: {.callout-note}
## Latent Unconfoundedness

$$\big( Y_{it=1}(0), Y_{it=2}(0) \big) \;\independent\; D_i \;\mid\; \eta_i$$

where $\eta_i$ is time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity (i.e., a unit fixed effect)

:::

* [Unconfoundedness]{.alert} - because this corresponds to the type of unconfoundedness that is very common for observational causal inference

* [Latent]{.alert-blue} - because the confounder is unobserved

## Motivating Parallel Trends

The most common way to "more primitively" motivate the parallel trends assumption is as a combination of the following two assumptions [@ashenfelter-card-1985;@angrist-krueger-1999;@ghanem-santanna-wuthrich-2024; @marx-tamer-tang-2025]:

::: {.callout-note}
## Latent Unconfoundedness

$$\big( Y_{it=1}(0), Y_{it=2}(0) \big) \;\independent\; D_i \;\mid\; \eta_i$$

where $\eta_i$ is time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity (i.e., a unit fixed effect)

:::

* Latent unconfoundedness says that we could recover $\ATT(d \mid d)$ if we could find units in dose group $d$ and untreated units with the same $\eta_i$ and compare their outcomes
* The previous comparison is infeasible, though, because $\eta_i$ is unobserved

## Motivating Parallel Trends {visibility="uncounted"}

The most common way to "more primitively" motivate the parallel trends assumption is as a combination of the following two assumptions [@ashenfelter-card-1985;@angrist-krueger-1999;@ghanem-santanna-wuthrich-2024; @marx-tamer-tang-2025]:

::: {.callout-note}
## Latent Unconfoundedness

$$\big( Y_{it=1}(0), Y_{it=2}(0) \big) \;\independent\; D_i \;\mid\; \eta_i$$

where $\eta_i$ is time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity (i.e., a unit fixed effect)

:::

* Alternatively, you can view this as "selection into being treated on time-invariant unobservables":
$$ \indicator{D_i > 0} = m_0(\eta_i) + u_{it} \text{ with } u_{it} \independent \big(Y_{it=1}(0), Y_{it=2}(0)\big) \bigm| \eta_i $$
* No restrictions on selection into a particular dose at all

## Motivating Parallel Trends {visibility="uncounted"}

The most common way to "more primitively" motivate the parallel trends assumption is as a combination of the following two assumptions [@ashenfelter-card-1985;@angrist-krueger-1999;@ghanem-santanna-wuthrich-2024; @marx-tamer-tang-2025]:

::: {.callout-note}

## Linear Model for Untreated Potential Outcomes

$$Y_{it}(0) = \theta_t + \eta_i + e_{it}$$

:::

* Under linearity of untreated potential outcomes, difference out $\eta_i$ and then parallel trends holds immediately by latent unconfoundedness
* However, these assumptions do not imply strong parallel trends---notice that the assumptions do not restrict potential outcomes $Y_{it=2}(d)$ for $d>0$ at all.

## Motivating Strong Parallel Trends

We can extend the notion of latent unconfoundedness as follows:

::: {.callout-note}
## Latent Unconfoundedness for Dose

$$\big\{Y_{i,t=1}(0),\, Y_{i,t=2}(d) : d \in \mathcal{D}\big\} \;\independent\; D_i \;\mid\; \eta_i$$
:::

* Extends latent unconfoundedness to holds for all potential outcomes, not just untreated ones
* Up to $\eta_i$ being unobserved, it is exactly the same assumption that you would see in the literature on continous treatment and dose response functions [@hirano-imbens-2004]
* If $\eta_i$ were observed, we could compare units with the same $\eta_i$ but different doses to recover $\ATT(d)$

## Motivating Strong Parallel Trends {visibility="uncounted"}

We can extend the notion of latent unconfoundedness as follows:

::: {.callout-note}
## Latent Unconfoundedness for Dose

$$\big\{Y_{i,t=1}(0),\, Y_{i,t=2}(d) : d \in \mathcal{D}\big\} \;\independent\; D_i \;\mid\; \eta_i$$
:::

* "Selection into dose on time-invariant unobservables":
$$D_i = m(\eta_i) + v_{it} \text{ with } v_{it} \independent \big(Y_{it=1}(0), Y_{it=2}(d) \big) \bigm| \eta_i$$
* Distribution of $\eta_i$ can systematically vary across dose groups, but other unobservables that affect potential outcomes cannot vary systematically across dose groups


## Motivating Strong Parallel Trends

We can also consider linear models for all potential outcomes:

::: {.callout-note}
## Linear Model for Potential Outcomes

$$Y_{i,t}(d) = \theta_{t,d} + \beta_{t,d} \,\eta_i + e_{i,t}(d)$$
:::

* Additive separability for parallel trends
* Coefficient on $\eta_i$ can vary with $t$ and/or $d$
* No tricks---this is exactly the same setup we would have in a linear model for potential outcomes if $\eta_i$ were observed

## School Closures Example

Back to Session 1's running example where $dose$ = length of Covid school closure, $outcome$ = test scores

* $\eta_i$: school's [unobserved student ability]{.alert-blue}

* $\theta_{t=2,d}$: the [ability-neutral]{.alert} part of the dose response, e.g., the component of lost instructional time/disruption that hits *any* school closed for length $d$, regardless of its students' baseline ability

* $\beta_{t=2,d}$: how strongly baseline ability $\eta_i$ [translates into]{.alert-green} test scores, *given* closure length $d$ --- i.e., varies with $d$ if high ability schools respond differently to different lengths of closures than low ability schools
  * Would be increasing in $d$ if high ability schools are more resilient to long closures than low ability schools.

## Does Strong Parallel Trends Hold in This Model? {visibility="uncounted"}

Applying the same argument as in Session 1:
$$
  \begin{aligned}
    \E[\Delta Y \mid D=d_h] - \E[\Delta Y \mid D=d_l] &= \ATT(d_h|d_h) - \ATT(d_l|d_l) \\
    &=  \underbrace{(\theta_{t=2,d_h} - \theta_{t=2,d_l}) + (\beta_{t=2,d_h} - \beta_{t=2,d_l}) \E[\eta \mid D=d_h]}_{\textrm{Causal Response}} \\
    &+ \underbrace{\beta_{t=2,d_l} \Big( \E[\eta \mid D=d_h] - \E[\eta \mid D=d_l] \Big)}_{\textrm{Selection Bias}}
  \end{aligned}
$$

* We would like for the selection bias term to be equal to 0.

* In particular, we will consider looking for dose groups where there is no selection (on the time-invariant unobservables) into the dose (i.e., $\E[\eta \mid D=d_h] - \E[\eta \mid D=d_l] = 0$).


# 2. Close Comparison Groups {visibility="uncounted"}

## Background

In @callaway-dyal-santanna-tsyawo-2025, we introduce a notion of "close comparison groups"

* Setting of that paper: binary treatment, multiple pre-treatment periods, multiple comparison groups, looking for a way to relax the parallel trends assumption, and we look for pockets of simple identification

* Groups that are "alike" in terms of pre-treatment levels of outcomes are "close comparison groups"

* If you can find such groups, you can get very robust identification of causal effects (i.e., robustness to the identification strategy)


## CCGs Adapted to a Continuous Treatment Setting

The idea here is that, if we can find range(s) of dose groups that are close comparison groups for each other (i.e., have the same pre-treatment level of outcomes), then it will suggest that strong parallel trends holds (locally) for those dose groups.


```{r echo=FALSE, results="asis"}

title <- "Close Comparsion Dose Groups"

before <- "Suppose we two dose groups $d_h$ and $d_l$ that have the same pre-treatment levels of outcomes, $$\\E[Y_{t=1} \\mid D=d_h] = \\E[Y_{t=1} \\mid D=d_l]$$

. . .

Then,

"

eqlist <- list("\\E[Y_{t=1} \\mid D=d_h] &= \\E[Y_{t=1}(0) \\mid D=d_h] = \\theta_1 + \\E[\\eta \\mid D=d_h]", "\\E[Y_{t=1} \\mid D=d_l] &= \\E[Y_{t=1}(0) \\mid D=d_l] = \\theta_1 + \\E[\\eta \\mid D=d_l]")

after <- "

. . .

Thus, close comparison dose groups satisfy:

$$\\E[Y_{t=1} \\mid D=l] = \\E[Y_{t=1} \\mid D=d] \\quad\\iff\\quad \\E[\\eta \\mid D=l] = \\E[\\eta \\mid D=d]$$

[If they have the same mean of $\\eta_i$, then the selection-bias terms above vanish, and strong parallel trends holds (at least locally)}{.alert}

"

step_by_step_eq(eqlist = eqlist,
  before = before,
  after = after,
  title = title)
```

## Implications

In a similar fashion to using pre-treatment periods to validate the parallel trends assumption, we can use pre-treatment periods to validate the "no selection"

* We can do this globally,
* Find regions where the pre-treatment mean is flat, or
* Find regions where the pre-treatment mean is flat conditional on covariates

It rationalizes interpreting those regions as being regions where strong parallel trends is plausible, and suggests that we can recover locally comparable causal effects in those regions, e.g., $\ACR(d)$ in these regions.

## Two More Realistic Versions of the Same Argument

Rather than "no selection at all," two weaker, more defensible versions deliver the same conclusion locally:

1. A [two-stage selection process]{.alert}: units select (or are sorted into) a coarse *category*, and dose only varies *within* category for reasons unrelated to $\eta_i$

2. Selection [on observables]{.alert}, some of which proxy for $\eta_i$: condition on $X_i$ and hope no *residual* selection on $\eta_i$ remains

## Version 1: Category, Then Noise

$D_i = d(C_i,\nu_i)$, where category $C_i$ carries the selection on $\eta_i$, and $\nu_i \independent \eta_i \mid C_i$ generates variation *within* category

* Two units with [different realized doses but the same category]{.alert-blue} are close comparison groups for each other --- regardless of the numeric gap between their doses

* Plausible whenever the dose isn't really a fine continuum in practice: a district picks a closure *stance* (short vs.\ extended remote learning), and the exact number of weeks within that stance is closer to scheduling noise; a state picks a minimum-wage *stance*, and the exact cents-per-hour within it is closer to legislative happenstance

* Less plausible for a genuinely continuous, deliberately-chosen dose

## Version 2: Covariates

Condition on observed $X_i$ (some of which may proxy for $\eta_i$) and define closeness *within* $X$-cells

* Same idea as before, but comparing $Y_{i,t=1} \mid D=l, X=x$ to $Y_{i,t=1} \mid D=d, X=x$

* Requires only that whatever selection on $\eta_i$ remains, it is absorbed by $X_i$ --- the familiar motivation behind [conditional]{.alert-blue} parallel trends, now stated as a within-cell closeness condition instead

## Side Comment: Does the Selection Model Match the Application?

A model like $D_i = m(\eta_i)+\nu_i$ presumes unit $i$ *actively chooses* its dose based on its own type --- often the wrong mental model

* For "exposure to a policy" designs (e.g., a hospital's dose = its *historical* Medicare share), $D_i$ is more mechanical/pre-determined than chosen --- better to directly ask about [balance of $\eta$]{.alert} across dose groups in the outcome model than to write down a choice model for $D_i$

## Side Comment: Aggregation Mismatch {visibility="uncounted"}

Many DiD applications observe disaggregated units, but the policy is chosen at a *more aggregated* level

* Example: Georgia raises its minimum wage more than Alabama. That choice is political, made at the [state]{.alert-blue} level --- e.g., GA having a large city may make pro-increase politicians more likely to be elected --- and has nothing *directly* to do with any one GA county's $\eta_i$

* It's plausible that, [conditional on a coarse covariate]{.alert} like rural/urban status, the distribution of $\eta$ across GA and AL *counties* is similar --- even though the state-level policy choice is clearly related to state-level characteristics

-->

## Application

Same empirical setting as Session 1:

* @acemoglu-finkelstein-2008's study of the 1983 Medicare PPS reform.
* Dose = hospital's pre-reform Medicare share
* outcome = capital-labor ratio (depreciation share)
* In session 1, we mainly looked at average outcomes before and after the treatment, but here we will use adjacent years instead, using 1982 as the base period.
  * Treatment effects: 1982 vs.\ 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986
  * Plus two more placebos marching up to 1982: 1980 vs.\ 1981, 1981 vs.\ 1982

## Pre-Test: ATT(d|d) {visibility="uncounted"}

[Two of three fail]{.alert} --- 1980-81 is close to 0, but 1981-82 ($\widehat{\ATT}=-0.22$) and 1982-83 ($\widehat{\ATT}=+0.20$) are both significant, in *opposite* directions

* 1982-83 could reflect anticipation: PPS was legislated in April 1983, months before its October 1983 effective date
* 1981-82 has no such story --- both years are firmly pre-treatment. This looks like genuine year-to-year instability, not just anticipation

[The flat region is remarkably stable]{.alert} across three separate years: roughly dose $0.35$ to $0.70$ in every one of 1980, 1981, and 1982

* This is what we'd expect if the flatness reflects a persistent hospital characteristic ($\eta_i$), not a fluke of any one year
* Use 1982's (largest) flat region as a single canonical "close comparison group" definition, applied everywhere next

## Summary of Application

It appears that:

1. Parallel trends seems to be violated in pre-treatment periods
2. Checking the levels of pre-treatment outcomes as a function of the dose suggested that there were pockets of no selection
3. Cross-dose comparisons are more likely to deliver causal effects in those pockets (i.e., a local version of strong parallel trends)
4. The estimates were noisy, and close to zero or slightly negative (substantially different than the positive estimates from the TWFE regression).  They don't provide any evidence that the Medicare policy increased capital labor ratios.

## Conclusion

Using pre-treatment periods to assess the plausibility of strong parallel trends is challenging because only untreated potential outcomes are observed in those periods.

However, the levels of outcomes in pre-treatment periods across different dose groups provides evidence about difference in the time-invariant unobservables driving their outcomes.

  * If differences in observed pre-treatment levels of outcomes are small, it suggests that differences in unobservables are small too.
  * If differences in unobservables are small, then strong parallel trends is more plausible, and cross-dose comparisons of trends in outcomes can be interpreted as approximately causal in those regions.
